strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine gap where existing UQ methods assume monotonic uncertainty accumulation, failing to capture how interactive agents reduce uncertainty through tool calls and clarification

Sound formal framework: Provides clear definitions (stochastic agent systems, agent UQ), unified graphical model capturing diverse prompting methods (ReAct, Reflexion), and shows existing approaches as special cases
Comprehensive scope: Discusses practical implications across healthcare, software engineering, and robotics; thoughtful treatment of limitations, ethical considerations, and open problems
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visualizations (Figures 1-4), concrete examples (flight booking), and systematic development from formulation to applications
Establishes research direction: Makes compelling case for why uncertainty in interactive agents requires fundamentally different conceptual thinking than static QA settings
weaknesses: Complete absence of empirical validation: No experiments, no real agent data, no demonstration that proposed framework improves uncertainty estimates or satisfies the desideratum (Eq. 1). Statement 'We leave actual implementation for future work' defers core contribution

Unresolved critical implementation challenges: Core components rely on notoriously difficult problems left unaddressed: (1) mutual information estimation (acknowledged as 'notorious for its difficulty'), (2) reliable action classification across domains (no methodology provided), (3) observation uncertainty estimation (authors admit 'will be much harder to estimate')

Unrealistic assumptions: Assumes reliable observations, deterministic environment transitions, and perfect action classification. Real agent environments violate these; limitations section acknowledges problems but provides no solutions

Circular reasoning in information gating: Gating function requires estimating Info(Oᵢ; O₀|Eᵢ\O₀), which is as hard as the original uncertainty estimation problem. No evidence this approach is more tractable than alternatives
Calibration gap unaddressed: Framework requires uncertainty predictive of task reward (Eq. 1), but modern LLMs are poorly calibrated. No discussion of achieving calibration; deferred to future work

Solution multiplicity problem undermines premise: Section 6 acknowledges cannot distinguish lack-of-knowledge from multiple-valid-actions. If indistinguishable, how does framework help? Fundamentally unresolved

Limited technical novelty: Dynamic Bayesian networks and chain-rule decomposition are standard. Main contribution is conceptual (gating mechanism) rather than technical. Epistemic vs. aleatoric uncertainty distinction well-known

Weak practical validation: Figure 3(a) uses synthetic examples only. No real agent trajectories. No data from deployed systems. Domain application claims (healthcare, robotics) are speculative without evidence

Lemma 1 provides limited actionability: Bounds are straightforward consequences, loose, and may not guide practical implementation. Why would theoretical bounds be more useful than direct uncertainty estimates?

Incomplete related work: Process reward modeling connection superficial. POMDP belief-tracking comparison unconvincing. Recent work on uncertainty propagation (Duan et al. 2025) insufficiently compared
